stages.title: Intermediate vocabulary
stages.hook: How would you describe today's weather to a friend in Turkish?
explain: Weather words: hava (weather, also air), güneş (sun), yağmur (rain), kar (snow), rüzgâr (wind), bulut (cloud), sıcak (hot) and soğuk (cold). To ask, say 'Hava nasıl?' (How is the weather?). The answer: 'Hava çok sıcak' or 'Yağmur yağıyor' (It is raining).

Notice that Turkish uses a verb for precipitation: yağmur yağıyor (rain is falling), kar yağıyor (snow is falling). The word yağmak means to fall as rain or snow. Seasons are ilkbahar (spring), yaz (summer), sonbahar (autumn) and kış (winter). 'Kışın kar yağar' (It snows in winter): kış and yaz take -ın (kışın, yazın), while ilkbahar and sonbahar take the usual -da (ilkbaharda, sonbaharda).
stages.mnemonic: Yağmur yağıyor, kar yağıyor: the sky does the verb 'yağmak'.

gq.q: Which verb is used with yağmur and kar?
gq.why: Yağmak is the verb for falling as rain or snow.

o: Who is outside in the cold?
gq.why: Hava means weather and nasıl means how.

panel.q: Why is it 'Kışın kar yağar' for a general truth?
o: It is the past tense, because winter has already ended
The aorist -ar describes habits and general facts
It is the future tense, because snow comes later
It is an order telling the snow to fall
panel.why: The aorist (geniş zaman) is used for general truths.

panel.q: Which ending shows 'in winter' in 'kışın'?
panel.why: Kış (winter) and yaz (summer) take -ın/-in to mean 'during that season': kışın, yazın. It is not the locative -de.

panel.q: A friend says 'Hava sıcak ama rüzgâr var'. What does this mean?
o: It is cold, and there is no wind at all
It is raining and the wind is strong
It is snowing and the air is hot
It is hot, but there is wind
panel.why: Ama means but; sıcak is hot; rüzgâr var means there is wind.

teach.model: Use hava for weather. For rain and snow use the verb yağmak: yağmur yağıyor. Winter and summer take -ın: kışın (in winter), yazın (in summer).

points.ask: What is weather?
What verb is used for rain?
How do I say 'in winter'?

trip.prompt: Find the regions and their typical weather.

stages.title: Verb forms and time expressions
stages.hook: How do you say 'I went', 'I go' and 'I will go' in Turkish?
explain: Turkish has clear suffixes for time. Past: -di (-dı, -du, -dü, -ti...): gittim (I went), geldim (I came), okudum (I read). Future: -ecek / -acak: gideceğim (I will go), okuyacağım (I will read). General or habitual: -ir / -ar: giderim (I go, I usually go).

Time words: dün (yesterday), bugün (today), yarın (tomorrow), geçen hafta (last week), gelecek hafta (next week), her gün (every day), bazen (sometimes), hiçbir zaman (never). After voiceless consonants -di becomes -ti: git-ti-m, not gid-di-m.
stages.mnemonic: Dün gittim, bugün gidiyorum, yarın gideceğim.

gq.q: Which sentence is in the past?
How do you say 'I will read'?
gq.why: The future is -acak plus the person ending.

panel.q: Why is it 'gittim' and not 'gitdim'?
o: Turkish does not allow the letter d after t in verbs
It is a typing mistake and gitdim is also fine
The verb git is irregular only in this one form
panel.why: Voiceless t in git triggers -ti.

panel.q: Why is the k in -ecek / -acak written ğ in 'geleceğim'?
o: Because the verb gelmek is irregular in the future
Because ğ is the English way of writing k
Because the letter k is silent in this suffix
Before a vowel ending the k softens to ğ
panel.why: Final k softens before vowel endings.

panel.q: Which verb form completes 'Yarın ...' (Tomorrow I ...)?
panel.why: Tomorrow needs the future: gideceğim.

teach.topic: Past, present and future in Turkish
teach.model: Past uses -di: gittim. Future uses -ecek/-acak: gideceğim. General habits use -ir/-ar. After a voiceless consonant -di becomes -ti.

points.ask: How do I make the past?
How do I make the future?
How do I talk about habits?

trip.prompt: Look at the tense endings and their examples.

stages.title: Complex sentence introduction
stages.hook: How can you join two ideas: 'I am tired' and 'I am going to the party'?
explain: Linking words build longer sentences: ve (and), ama (but), çünkü (because), bu yüzden (so, that is why), eğer ... -sa (if). Example: 'Yorgunum ama partiye gidiyorum' (I am tired but I am going to the party).

Turkish often uses endings instead of 'because': 'Yağmur yağdığı için evde kaldım' (Because it rained, I stayed home). The easier form is 'çünkü': 'Evde kaldım çünkü yağmur yağıyordu.' Conditional: 'Yağmur yağarsa evde kalırım' (If it rains, I will stay at home), with -sa / -se on the verb.
sentences: I stayed home because it rained.
If it rains, I stay home.

panel.q: Why does 'Yağmur yağarsa' mean 'if it rains'?
o: Because yağmak itself means 'if' in Turkish
Because yağmur is a verb in the past tense
Because the ending -ar always means a question
panel.why: The conditional suffix -sa/-se means if.

panel.q: Which sentence correctly joins two clauses with a contrast?
panel.why: Ama joins the contrast between tired and going.

panel.q: Which conjunction gives the same meaning as the ending in 'yağdığı için' (because it rained)?
panel.why: -dığı için and çünkü both give the reason.

teach.model: Use ve for and, ama for but, çünkü for because, and -sa for if. Reasons can also use için after a verb noun.

points.ask: How do I say but?
How do I say because?
How do I say if?

trip.prompt: Compare how Turkish uses endings and conjunctions.

stages.title: Reading short stories
stages.hook: How does a Turkish fairy tale begin?
explain: Many Turkish tales begin 'Bir varmış, bir yokmuş' (Once there was, once there was not), a formula that hints we are in a story world. The ending -miş marks reported or storytelling tense: 'Bir adam varmış' (There was a man, it is said).

A well-known folk figure is Nasreddin Hoca, who appears in short, funny stories where logic is turned upside down. Reading short stories, find: who (kim), where (nerede), what happened (ne oldu) and why (neden). Typical story words: bir gün (one day), sonra (then), en sonunda (finally), mutlu son (happy end).
stages.mnemonic: Bir varmış, bir yokmuş: the -miş says 'they say'.

gq.q: What does the ending -miş suggest in a story?
Which phrase opens many Turkish fairy tales?
gq.why: It is the classic tale opening.

panel.q: Why do tale tellers use -miş and not -di?
o: They did not see events and report what is said
They are speaking to children only, and -di is for adults
-di is never used in tales because it is too formal
-miş is the future and tales are about what comes next
panel.why: Evidential -miş marks hearsay.

panel.q: A story says 'sonra ... en sonunda'. What does this show?
panel.why: Time connectors give sequence.

panel.q: Nasreddin Hoca stories mainly use which technique?
o: Long speeches in the language of the courts
Mathematical proofs that end in a puzzle
Short humorous anecdotes with a twist
Scientific reports about animals and plants
panel.why: They are brief funny stories with a wise twist.

teach.model: Tales begin with Bir varmış, bir yokmuş. -miş shows something told, not seen. Look for who, where, what happened and why.

points.ask: What does -miş mean in a tale?
How does a tale start?
Who is Nasreddin Hoca?

trip.prompt: Read an anecdote and find the joke.

stages.title: Listening comprehension
stages.hook: If someone says 'Toplantı üçte', what time is the meeting?
explain: When you listen, catch numbers, places and times. 'Toplantı saat üçte' is 'The meeting is at three o'clock'. 'Yarın sabah dokuzda' is 'Tomorrow morning at nine'. Turkish times use -de/-da: dörtte (at four), beşte (at five).

Listening tips: the stress is on the last syllable, the verb comes at the end, and short words (ve, de, mi) are not stressed. If you miss something say 'Pardon?' or 'Tekrar eder misiniz?'. To check the main idea first, ask: kim, ne, nerede, ne zaman?
stages.mnemonic: Hear kim, ne, nerede, ne zaman before you hear the details.

panel.q: Why is it 'üçte' and not 'üçde'?
o: Because the word üç is irregular in Turkish
Because üç is a verb that takes a special ending
Because -de is only used in some dialects
panel.why: Ç is voiceless, so -te is used.

panel.q: Which listening strategy helps most with a fast phone message?
o: Translate each word one by one into English
Ignore the numbers and listen for the tune
Listen first for who, what, where and when
Wait until the end and then decide what it meant
panel.why: Key questions give the main idea.

panel.q: You hear 'Toplantı yarın sabah dokuzda'. When is it?
o: Today at nine o'clock in the evening
Next week on Monday at nine
Tomorrow at nine in the morning
panel.why: Yarın is tomorrow, sabah is morning, dokuz is nine.

teach.model: Listen for who, what, where and when. Time uses -de or -te: üçte, dörtte. If you miss it, ask Tekrar eder misiniz?

points.ask: What do I listen for?
How do I say 'at three'?
How do I ask to repeat?

trip.prompt: Practise by listening to a short announcement.

stages.title: Conversation and pronunciation
stages.hook: Why does the stress often fall on the last syllable in Turkish?
explain: Turkish words are normally stressed on the last syllable: ma-SA, ki-TAP, ar-ka-DAŞ. When you add endings, the stress moves: masa, masaLAR, masalarIM. Some place names are exceptions, for example AN-ka-ra, with stress on the first syllable.

Speak in even beats and keep vowels pure: Turkish vowels do not glide like English. Practise ı and ö: 'ışık', 'göz'. Say ü like the French u (lips rounded). The negative -me/-ma pulls the stress onto the syllable just before it: GEL-me-di (he did not come).
stages.mnemonic: Last syllable is the loudest; when you add a suffix, the loud part moves.
sentences: The bird is singing in the garden.

gq.q: Where does the stress usually fall in Turkish words?
gq.why: Turkish word stress is usually final.

o: Like the English oo in 'moon', with the lips pushed forward
Like a short e, with the lips spread wide
With rounded lips, like the French u
Like a dotted i, with the tongue pulled back
gq.why: Ü is a front rounded vowel.

panel.q: What happens to stress when you add the plural: masa → masalar?
o: It stays on the first syllable: MA-sa-lar
It disappears when the plural ending is added
It moves to the end: ma-sa-LAR
It jumps to the first syllable of the new word
panel.why: Final stress moves with the suffix.

panel.q: A learner says 'gül' as 'gul'. What is the problem?
o: The consonant g is said like English j
The stress is on the wrong syllable here
The word has been shortened in speech
The vowel ü is replaced by u
panel.why: ü and u are different vowels.

panel.q: Where does the stress fall in 'gelmedi' (he did not come)?
o: On gel, the syllable before the negative -me
On the last syllable, which is always stressed in Turkish
On the negative suffix -me itself, as in many languages
Nowhere: negative verbs are said without stress
panel.why: The negative suffix -me/-ma pulls the stress onto the syllable just before it, so the word is said GEL-me-di, not gel-me-DI.

teach.model: Stress is usually on the last syllable. Endings move it. Say ü and ö with rounded lips and keep vowels pure.

points.ask: Where does the stress go?
How do I say ü and ö?
What happens when I add an ending?

stages.title: Writing paragraphs
stages.hook: How do you write a paragraph that has a beginning, a middle and an end?
explain: A good short paragraph has a topic sentence, details, and an ending. Useful linking words: önce (first), sonra (then), daha sonra (later), en sonunda (finally), bu yüzden (therefore). Example: 'Dün sabah erken kalktım. Önce kahvaltı yaptım. Sonra okula gittim. Akşam eve döndüm.'

In Turkish writing, keep the past tense steady: kalktım, yaptım, gittim, döndüm. Start sentences with a capital letter and end with a full stop. Commas separate clauses. Check your suffixes: -de/-te, -dan/-ten, and the vowel harmony of each ending.
stages.mnemonic: First, then, later, finally: önce, sonra, daha sonra, en sonunda.
sentences: In the evening I returned home.

gq.q: Which word shows the first step?
Which tense is natural for retelling yesterday?

panel.q: Why check -de and -te in your paragraph?
o: They mean different things, such as place and time
Turkish has no fixed rules for these endings
It is only a question of style, not of grammar
The ending depends on the last sound of the word
panel.why: -de/-te choice follows voiceless sounds.

panel.q: Which order is logical for a morning routine?
o: Önce kalktım, sonra kahvaltı yaptım, en sonunda okula gittim
En sonunda kalktım, önce okula gittim, sonra kahvaltı yaptım
Sonra kalktım, önce kahvaltı yaptım, en sonunda okula gittim
Kahvaltı yaptım, sonra kalktım, en sonunda okula gittim
panel.why: Linking words show sequence.

panel.q: What makes a paragraph clear?
o: Only very long words and complicated sentences
Only questions that the reader must answer
No punctuation, so that the text flows quickly
panel.why: Structure and connectors help the reader.

teach.model: Begin with a topic sentence. Link with önce, sonra, daha sonra, en sonunda. Keep one tense and check endings.

points.ask: What linking words can I use?
Which tense do I keep?
What do I check at the end?

trip.prompt: See how a paragraph is structured.

stages.title: Cultural expressions and idioms
stages.hook: Why do Turks say 'Eline sağlık' after a meal?
explain: Turkish has many fixed expressions. 'Eline sağlık' (health to your hand) thanks a cook. 'Kolay gelsin' (may it be easy) is said to someone working. 'Geçmiş olsun' wishes recovery. 'Hayırlı olsun' congratulates on a new job or house. 'Çok yaşa' is said after a sneeze, and the sneezer answers 'Sen de gör'.

Some idioms use body parts: 'gözüm üstünde' (my eye is on it, I will gladly do it), 'başım üstüne' (on my head, with pleasure). 'Elini çabuk tut' means 'be quick'. Such expressions are not translated word for word; learn the situation they belong to.
stages.mnemonic: Eline sağlık for cooks, kolay gelsin for workers.
sentences: May it be easy for you.

gq.q: What do you say to a person who cooked?

gq.why: It is a greeting to workers.

panel.q: Why is 'Eline sağlık' not 'Thank you, your hand is healthy'?
o: It is a fixed expression with a cultural meaning
It is grammatically wrong and should not be used
It is slang that only young people say
It is a question about a person's health
panel.why: Idioms are learned as units.

panel.q: A neighbour moves house. Which phrase is best?
panel.why: It congratulates a new beginning.

panel.q: Someone is ill. Which phrase fits?
panel.why: It wishes recovery.

teach.model: Learn phrases for situations: Eline sağlık (thanks to cook), Kolay gelsin (to workers), Geçmiş olsun (get well). Do not translate word for word.

points.ask: When do I say Eline sağlık?
When do I say Kolay gelsin?
When do I say Geçmiş olsun?

stages.title: Practical travel communication
stages.hook: You are at a bus station in Turkey. How do you buy a ticket to İzmir?
explain: Useful travel phrases: 'Bir bilet lütfen' (One ticket please), 'İzmir'e bir bilet' (A ticket to İzmir), 'Otogar nerede?' (Where is the bus station?), 'Havaalanı' (airport), 'tren' (train), 'otobüs' (bus). The dative ending -e/-a means to: İzmir'e, Ankara'ya.

Staying: 'Bir oda istiyorum' (I want a room), 'Kaç gece?' (How many nights?), 'Hesap lütfen' (The bill, please). If you need help, say 'Yardım eder misiniz?'. In cities, many people use the İstanbulkart for buses, ferries and metro. Politely start with 'Affedersiniz' (Excuse me).
sentences: Excuse me, where is the bus station?
I want a room for two nights.

gq.q: Which phrase asks for the bill?

panel.q: Why is it 'İzmir'e' and 'Ankara'ya'?
o: They are different cities with different grammar rules
Ankara ends in a vowel, so a buffer y is added
The choice between e and ya is random
Ankara is a verb, so it takes the other ending
panel.why: After a vowel -e/-a uses -ye/-ya.

panel.q: Which is the most polite way to start a request?
panel.why: Affedersiniz is polite.

panel.q: A hotel clerk asks 'Kaç gece?'. What do they want to know?
panel.why: Kaç gece means how many nights.

teach.model: Use Bir bilet lütfen for tickets, Otogar nerede? for directions and Hesap lütfen for the bill. Direction uses -e/-a: İzmir'e.

points.ask: How do I buy a ticket?
How do I ask where?
How do I say 'to a city'?

trip.prompt: Look for the main modes of transport.
